Welcome

The purpose of this handbook is to introduce you to the Passages Program. Reading and understanding this handbook will improve the residential experience. At the end, there will be a celebration of your knowledge and an opportunity to show your understanding of the program and expectations. Additionally, there is a place for your parent or guardian to sign off that they reviewed the handbook as well.


We are a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF), located inside of Brynn Marr Hospital. We follow policy and procedures of Brynn Marr Hospital. However, as a PRTF, there are also other operations that you will need to understand to be successful in the program.


Most of the adolescent girls who attend our program are here between four and six months. During that time, you will be involved in creating a Master Treatment Plan that directs the course of your treatment. There are services we offer to enhance your treatment, including: medication management; individual, group, and family therapies; recreational therapy; behavior management; nursing group and monitoring; psychiatric observations; and individualized school programming. We feature evidence based models of treatment including but not limited to Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Dialectical Behavioral Therapy. We will also engage you in fun activities such as monthly events and seasonal celebrations. Currently, we view treatment issues through a “trauma lens”, focusing on your strengths and abilities.


Mission Statement


Passages is a Psychiatric Residential Treatment Facility (PRTF) providing behavioral, therapeutic, and transitional supports in a structured and secured environment. We strive to foster personal growth to assist with building skills that will enhance relationships, academic performance, and the activities of daily living. We are committed to developing young women who are responsible, respectful, and contributing members of their communities and families.


Before we go on further, let us introduce you to the treatment guides who will assist you throughout your journey.

Trauma Informed Mission:


At Brynn Marr, we believe in the implementation of seven elements to achieve a Trauma Informed Care Organization.

  1. Understanding the PREVALENCE of trauma.

  2. Teaching the IMPACT of trauma.

  3. Achieving a PERSPECTIVE SHIFT.

  4. Assisting, teaching and achieving REGULATION.

  5. Developing and believing in the power of RELATIONSHIPS.

  6. Helping to find for our employees consumers a REASON FOR BEING

  7. Supporting CAREGIVER CAPACITY


Trauma Informed Principles

Safety: Ensure physical and emotional safety, recognizing and responding to how racial, ethnic, religious, gender and/or sexual identity may impact safety across the lifespan.


Trustworthiness: Foster genuine relationships and practices that build trust, making tasks clear, maintaining appropriate boundaries and creating norms for interaction that promote reconciliation and healing. Understand and respond to ways in which explicit and implicit power can affect the development of trusting relationships. This includes acknowledging and mitigating internal biases and recognizing the historic power of majority populations.


Choice: Maximize choice, addressing how privilege, power, and historic relationships impact both perceptions about and ability to act upon choice.


Collaboration: Honor transparency and self-determination, and seek to minimize the impact of the inherent power differential while maximizing collaboration and sharing responsibility for making meaningful decisions.


Empowerment: Encouraging self-efficacy, identifying strengths and building skills which leads to individual pathways for healing while recognizing and responding to the impact of historical trauma and oppression.


What is Trauma Informed Care?


Realizes wide impact of trauma and understands potential pathways to recovery;

Recognizes the signs and symptoms of trauma in children/youth, families and staff;

Responds by fully integrating knowledge in policies, practices and environments; and

Seeks to actively resist re-traumatization


Research indicates that maintaining a presence within the milieu, noticing early changes within the patient and the therapeutic setting, assessing the patient with early intervention, utilizing less restrictive measures, and changing aspects of the milieu helps to promote a culture of structure, calmness, and collaboration rather than control promotes a decrease in restraint and seclusion outcomes. This includes fewer injuries, shorter lengths of stay, decreased recidivism/re-hospitalization, less medication use and increased positive outcomes/discharges with higher level of functioning at the time of discharge.


The Guides on Your Journey

The Multidisciplinary Team


You (The Resident) & Your Supports

YOU are the center of your treatment. It is up to you to use the information and skills you will be taught by your treatment team to improve the way you think and behave. Your family is required to be involved throughout your treatment to provide you with the most support to ensure you the greatest success.

Psychiatric Services

Your medical provider is the leader of your treatment team. They assess your mood and mental status. Your provider is responsible for all treatment orders, such as medication, tests, and Therapeutic Trial Visits (TTV). You will have the chance to talk with them regularly and give feedback related to how you are feeling, how you feel like you are progressing in treatment, and how your medications are supporting your psychiatric needs.

Program Therapists

Your program therapist oversees your programming to ensure you are receiving a well-rounded therapeutic plan of care. The therapist will provide you with individual, group, and family therapies. You will be individually assigned a therapist. They will be the primary contact person to speak with your family throughout your treatment.


Nursing

Your nurse supervises your day-to-day care on the unit and is responsible for educating you on medications and health issues. Your nurse also shares information regarding your daily response to treatment with the rest of the treatment team.

Recreational Therapists

The Recreational Therapists will provide you with opportunities to participate in fun activities. These activities will focus on creative expression and the development and application of appropriate social and relaxation skills to improve communication of emotions, wants, and needs with art and movement.


Education Department

Village Academy provides an on-site educational program utilizing two Masters educated licensed teachers. The Principal is responsible for overseeing your academic needs and will provide academic goals to you. Communication with your home school at the time of admission, during your treatment at Passages Transformations, and upon discharge from the residential program will be supported to encourage continuity of educational goals.

Mental Health Technicians

Your Mental Health Technicians (MHTs) work with the nurse in supervising your day-to-day activities. Your MHTs facilitate various groups and work closely with you in managing your daily functioning and your behaviors.





Dress Code Guidelines

  • Clothing must be in good repair (no holes) and good taste. Shorts must be at least knee length.

  • Clothing/items with drug, alcohol, satanic, violence, gang, or sexually inappropriate themes are not considered appropriate.

  • Skirts are not permitted.

  • As a safety precaution, belts and ties in clothing cannot be worn.

  • Sleeping caps can only be worn at night in the resident’s bedroom.

  • Pants must be buttoned and cannot sag.

  • Shoes must be worn at all times, unless otherwise indicated.

  • Weather-appropriate clothing is expected when going outdoors.

  • Sunglasses, hoods, gloves or hats are not permitted to be worn in the facility.

  • Clothing or items prohibited by these guidelines will be stored for family members to pick up on the next visit.


Other Guidelines

  • Hygiene products cannot contain alcohol as the first 2 ingredients, have a pump or be larger than 12 oz.

  • Residents cannot borrow or lend clothing or other personal belongings to other residents.


PLEASE NOTE: It would be very difficult to list every rule in the handbook so you must always remember that the staff members who are caring for you will let you know the expectations and you need to listen to them and do as they ask.

Focus on Your Treatment. There is a reason that you have come to Passages. Our goal is to assist you as you evaluate why you are in treatment and what changes need to happen in your life so things can be better. Much of this work will be done through individual and family therapy. You will have goals for your sessions with your therapist. These goals are to help you look at your past and how it has affected you as well as to help you consider how you want your life to be different going forward. Working on your treatment includes many other things:


  • Listening and participating in groups including but not limited to Recreational Therapy, Life Skills, Psycho Ed., Group Therapy, School, etc. Groups are an important part of your treatment. Staff will work hard to help you with your treatment when planning these groups. Open yourself up to learning how to improve things in your life.

  • You will oftentimes be given assignments to work on related to your treatment. Take these seriously and consider the information you are asked to share.

  • Work closely with your therapist to develop goals and plans for your treatment that will help things improve for you once you discharge from the Passages Program.

  • Work in individual therapy with your therapist to consider the things in your life that you are struggling with and make a plan for what can be done to make things better.

  • Talk with your parents/guardians about how things can improve outside of the facility. Be an active participant in making a plan for your life and the lives of those around you to be better.

  • Remember that you are always working on your treatment in every aspect of your day at Passages.

  • Focus on yourself and not on your peers.


Use Positive Coping Skills. This allows you to learn and practice new ways of dealing with feelings and stress in an appropriate, safe, and socially acceptable manner. Look at treatment like a personal “practice field,” a place to try out new positive skills learned and the ability to identify and continue using what helps the best.

  • Use positive strategies to cope with feelings and frustrations. You will develop these during treatment.

  • Ask for personal time, (Take 5), if you need to refocus. Please note: if you do not request to Take 5 BEFORE walking out, it will count as programming refusal. When you are done, staff will process with you, how you are feeling and what was happening to cause you to need to Take 5.

  • Focus on completing your individualized treatment goals.

  • Listen to what others are saying and consider their feedback as you try and deal with your feelings and emotions appropriately.

  • Let others know how you feel rather than blaming when you are struggling with something.

  • Ignore negative behavior from others. Just because someone else isn’t choosing to work on their treatment doesn’t mean you should follow their lead. If others are trying to drag you down with them by saying or doing things that upset you, you are encouraged to ignore this. Don’t allow them to control how you are working your treatment program.

  • Accept consequences and feedback for negative choices appropriately. Sometimes we have to be reminded of problem behaviors or areas in which we are not dealing with treatment appropriately. Being able to listen to this feedback is important as it will help you improve. It is okay to make mistakes or not always make the right choice, it’s how you handle the consequence of our choices that is important.

  • Use positive language and refrain from cursing.



Program overview

The Passages program is a behavioral management program that teaches “real life” skills needed to successfully make appropriate and healthy choices while navigating through the healing process of trauma.

Your “job” is identifying the triggers that lead to impulsive, defiant and sometimes aggressive behavior and learning the skill of choosing and utilizing realistic coping skills to successfully navigate obstacles.

The Passages program levels the playing field allowing each resident the opportunity to succeed regardless of trauma, past choices and social status. As long as you put in the work, the rewards will come.

Your daily schedule is broken up into small increments for which you receive points for positive behavior choices. Three prompts to correct behavior are to be given before the decision is made to not award points. However, the number of prompts allowed will lessen as you advance in phases. Earned points may not be taken away. The point sheets are reviewed with you every night after dinner during a Goals wrap up group. Questions regarding behavior choices and possible better choices should be discussed.

You will receive a weekly paycheck for your work towards positive behavioral choices and go through the banking process to cash your check and receive the appropriate amount of Brynn Marr Bucks.

These “Bucks” can be used for a variety of things. They can purchase time in the incentive lounge, be spent at the incentive store and pay for outings and events to name only a few.

As you progress from phase to phase, you will receive a pay increase. In order to “Phase up”, you will need to have successfully completed your individual phase packet and in writing, request to meet with the treatment team via a “Phase up request”.

Our Programming Model

Here, at Passages, we utilize a PHASE SYSTEM. It consists of six phases.

Orientation – Making a Commitment to Treatment

Phase I – Safety, Stability, and Skills Development

Phase II – Show Competency and Symptom Reduction

Phase III – Demonstration of Independent Skills Use

Phase IV – Finding Joy, Meaning, and Strong Sense of Self Awareness




Orientation - Making a Commitment to Treatment

When you are first admitted you begin the program on Orientation. On this level you are expected to begin identifying the behaviors that led to you admission to the program; learn the program rules; become familiar with the Point and Level Systems as well as Brynn Marr Bucks.


This is the time for you and the staff to get to know one another. You will be oriented to the program, given information about the unit rules and schedules, and be introduced to peers and staff.


Expectations:

  • Read and understand the Handbook.

  • Pass a quiz about the program.

  • Comply with all unit rules and take medications as prescribed.

  • Demonstrate safety for self, others, and property.

  • Keep room and personal belongings neat and clean.

  • Cooperate and follow staff directions.

  • Show respect for self, peers, staff, and guests.

  • Bedtime 9:00 pm. Lights out 9:30 pm.

Privileges:

  • One 15 minute phone call on days assigned according to your room number

  • Weekend visitation with your family members

  • Television during scheduled times.

  • Accumulates 3 Brynn Marr Bucks per week towards weekly incentive Store

  • Bedtime at 9:00 pm. Lights out at 9:30 pm



Criteria for Advancement to Phase I:

May advance to Phase I when the following criteria are met:

  1. Has met all of the above expectations for Entry Level.

  2. Has been on Entry Level a minimum of 7 Days.

  3. Not an Elopement risk.

  4. Decrease life threatening behaviors and demonstrate a commitment to treatment.


PHASE I - Safety, Stability, and Skills Development

During phase I, it is expected that identify and acknowledge the thoughts, the feelings, and the behaviors that brought you into the Passages program.

While on Phase I, you are expected to begin to demonstrate impulse control. You are beginning to show responsible behaviors.

Expectations:

All expectations from Entry Level plus the following:

  • Cooperate and follow staff direction with no more than three prompts.

  • Attend and participate in school without disruption and without walking out of class without permission

  • Begin to work on identified goals

  • Have a clear understanding of the handbook

  • Work with your therapist to develop treatment goals for your treatment plan

  • Complete written assignment and review with your therapist:

  • Phase I Packet – Individualized to meet your needs as pertains to your Treatment goals

Privileges:

  • One 15 minute phone call on days assigned according to your room number

  • Weekend visitation with your family members

  • Television during scheduled times.

  • Accumulates 3 Brynn Marr Bucks per week towards weekly incentive Store

  • Bedtime at 9:00 pm. Lights out at 9:30 pm



Criteria for Advancement to Phase II:

  1. Has met all of the expectations for Phase I

  2. Completion of Individualized Packet created by Treatment Team with your therapist

  3. Has been on Phase I a minimum of 25 programming days prior to requesting a petition from your Program Facilitator.

  4. Approval by Clinical Team



PHASE II - Show Competency and Symptom Reduction

During this period, it is expected that you continue to build on what you’ve learned about thoughts, feelings, and behaviors that brought you into the program.

On this level you are expected to show responsible behavior on and off the unit. You are expected to demonstrate your continued commitment the program and improved communication of emotions, wants and needs.

Expectations:

All expectations from Entry Level, Phase I plus the following:

  • Cooperate and follow staff direction with no more than one prompts.

  • Show appropriate behaviors in different social environments (Ex. School, cafeteria, outings, etc.)

  • Complete written assignments:

  • Phase II packet - Individualized to meet your needs as pertains to your Treatment goals

Privileges:

All privileges from Entry Level, Phase I plus the following:

  • Able to earn Incentive Lounge time

  • Ability to earn 6 Brynn Marr Bucks weekly towards weekly incentive store

  • Eligible for outings and community Therapeutic Trial Visits (TTV)



Criteria for Advancement to Phase III:

  1. Completion of Phase II Packet with your therapist

  2. Has been on Phase II a minimum of 30 programming days before presenting your petition to the Clinical Team

  3. Has demonstrated safe behavior for self and others

  4. Addresses feelings and thoughts openly and honestly without being superficial (pretending by saying what the listener wants to hear, being “fake,” Saying the “right things” without meaning it.

  5. Has been addressing therapeutic issues and goals in therapies and activities in an open and honest manner.

  6. Has met short term treatment goals identified on Treatment Plan

  7. Demonstrating appropriate role model skills and behaviors

  8. Complete a minimum of the last seven consecutive days of keeping 90% of your points prior to petitioning for Phase advancement

  9. Approval by Clinical Team


PHASE III - Demonstration of Independent Skills Use

Phase III is made up of the next 30 days of programming. During this period, it is expected that you will ask yourself the questions “Who am I?” and “Why am I here?”

On this level you will demonstrate that not only can you live within the program rules but that you are making an honest effort to work on your problem behaviors. On Phase III you are also actively showing a willingness to work on the difficulties between you and your family that led to your admission to the program. You are receptive to feedback regarding you behavior and actively work towards resolving conflicts with others that supports improved opportunities of success following discharge.

Expectations:

Consistently meet all expectations from Entry Level, Phase I, Phase II plus the following:

  • Consistently show appropriate social skills behavior

  • Work on individual and family issues

  • Consistently keep room and belongings clean and neat

  • Consistently attend school without disruption and complete assignments

  • Consistently follow staff directions without prompts.

  • Consistently working and showing improvement on long-term goals by achieving short-term goals

  • While on outing or TTV, demonstrate the same personal responsibility and willingness to work on difficult issues the same as expected on unit

  • Evidence of willingness to be helpful to others including being appropriately supportive and assertive, both in activities and on unit

  • Discuss treatment issues, feelings, and thoughts in an open and honest manner

  • Demonstrate appropriate role model skills and behaviors by mentoring new residents

  • Demonstrate the ability to use healthy coping skills

  • Complete Phase 3 Packet – Individualized to meet your needs as pertains to your Treatment goals


Privileges:

All privileges from Entry Level, Phase I, Phase II, plus the following:

  • Eligible for outings and overnight Therapeutic Trial Visits (TTV)

  • Extended bedtimes on weekends with TV privileges

  • Friday night special snack

  • Ability to earn 9 Brynn Marr Bucks weekly to use in the weekly incentive store


Criteria for Advancement to Phase IV:

    1. Has met all of the above expectations for Phase III

    2. Transition Level minimum of 21 days

    3. Approval by Clinical Team



PHASE IV - Finding Joy, Meaning, and Strong Sense of Self Awareness

This is the final phase is when you ask the question “Where do I go from here?” It is a time of putting into action everything you have learned in order to determine if you are ready to face the challenges of staying on your path when you don’t have the daily input and feedback of a treatment program. You will have learned a great deal and you will have put it into practice while at Passages, but now you will face new and additional challenges as you return to your community environment.

In using the knowledge and understanding that you gained in the second and third phases, you will be encouraged to more independently use the skills you have developed in order to manage your feelings and behaviors in an appropriate manner. You will continue to participate in the behavior modification system. You will continue to use the coping skills you have developed and been successfully using. The members of your team will give you feedback on how you are doing. In this Phase, more will be expected of you. You have been given the tools to help you manage your feelings and now is the time to determine if you can use those skills on your own. You will have the opportunities to problem solve using your newly learned skills. You will be challenged to display those things you have learned by demonstrating stability on a consistent basis.

During this final phase, you will be developing personal longer term goals for yourself. You will develop a road map of your life and how you would like it to turn out. You will develop a plan for ensuring that you meet your goals.

On this level you will demonstrate the ability to function as a consistent, responsible member of the community. You will demonstrate trustworthiness and a helpful, cooperative relationship with the staff, as well as a willingness to reach out actively to others in the program. You are able to recognize the needs of others as well as your own needs.

You are capable and willing to serve as a role model and to actively participate in finding constructive solutions to problems as they arise.

Expectations:

Consistently model expected behaviors from Entry Level, Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, plus the following:

  • Consistently work on individual goals

  • Consistently follow all rules without a prompt

  • Complete written assignments as required

  • Demonstrate positive leadership skills

  • Assist in choosing activities and incentives for programming

  • Demonstrate responsible behavior in ongoing effort to work things out at home, on the unit and on extended TTVs

  • Willingness to exercise a role in leadership, such as co-leading Goal groups, organizing special functions/activities, orienting new patients to unit, programs, etc.

  • Serve as a role model to your peers on the unit

  • Continue to display behaviors that demonstrate all that you have learned

  • Consistently maintain appropriate behaviors on the unit and at home



Privileges:

All privileges from Phase I, Phase II, Phase III, plus the following:

    • Assist staff as needed as requested with specific tasks

    • Preferred seating

    • First in line for snacks and events such as incentive store

    • Offsite events

    • Assists RT in activities (planning)

    • Therapeutic Trial Visits

Goals:

  • Complete a behavioral agreement with your guardians

  • Write a personal mission statement (who you are, what’s important to you, what your history is and how you are changing)

  • Write a personal vision statement in detail stating where you live, work, go to school and what you want your life to look like 5 years from now

  • Relapse Prevention Plan


Therapeutic Trial Visits (TTVs)

Residents who have successfully advanced to the third week of Phase 3 will be evaluated for participating in therapeutic trial visits (TTV) with their guardians/family members in order to allow them to work together on their treatment goals. These TTVs will range in time from 4-6 hours. 24+ hours are only available at the end of Phases 4, depending on treatment goals, family location, patient’s stability, etc. Opportunities for time in the home environment are extremely important during these Phases. Longer periods of time spent in the home environment provide more opportunities to put into practice the skills that have been learned in individual, group, family, and milieu therapies. These evaluation periods are vital as the Passages Treatment Team determine when a patient is ready for discharge.

TTV’s can and will be forfeited in the event of unsafe, inappropriate, negative behaviors in or outside of the facility.

Expected behaviors for TTV eligibility:

  • Active participation in individual, family, and/or group therapy

  • Active participation in all school activities

  • Appropriate responses to staff redirection

  • Free from physical aggression and aggressive verbal interactions with parents/guardians, staff, and/or peers

  • Free from self-harming behaviors

  • Maintaining the identified criteria for each Phase




Prompts

Orientation and Phase I - no more than three prompts.

Phase II – no more than one prompt

Phase III and IV – NO prompts


ELIGIBILITY FOR WEEKLY INCENTIVE CUTOFF

Orientation: 3 Yellow or 2 Red

Phase I: 2 Yellow or 2 Red

Phase II: 2 Yellow or 1 Red

Phase III: 2 Yellow

Phase IV: 1 Yellow

G etting Past the Cloudy Days



Before The Rain, Remember To…

Stop what you are doing or “Freeze”

Think about the consequences: Is it worth it?

Act make the right choice and use positive coping skills

Plan what you can do differently next time

We all get triggered sometimes, but you have to learn to cope with the stressors of life. Your staff will make every effort to help you cool off, but you also have to help yourself also. If you are upset and need to calm down, your first plan should be to use your coping skills (such as deep breaths, pacing, journaling, etc.). You can also choose to talk to someone about how you are feeling. If these don’t work for you and you end up requiring additional help to make sure that you aren’t a danger to yourself or others, the following interventions might be used:

1:1 - This is a brief discussion with the unit nurse or staff regarding your thoughts and feelings about something that concerns you. Your nurse or unit staff may direct you to your therapist for further assistance.

Take 5: - So as not to lose control in an upsetting situation, you may voluntarily remove yourself from that situation and find yourself a “safe-place” where you can calm down privately. The expectation is that you will discuss the situation after you have calmed in order to evaluate coping skills used. If you need to “Take 5” during a structured activity (Ex. school, groups, RT, etc.), you must first communicate your need with staff before walking out. Please note: if you do not request to Take 5 BEFORE walking out, it will count as programming refusal. When you are done, staff will process with you, how you are feeling and what was happening to cause you to need to Take 5.

Refocus Time – If you are unable or unwilling to recognize that you need time away from the group, the staff may ask you to take some time to refocus. This time can be up to 10 minutes in duration, unless otherwise stated on your treatment plan. Your time will begin when you are quiet and able to reflect on your behavior.

Reflection Time/Room Refocus – If you are continually struggling to manage your behaviors, you may be asked to spend up to one hour in a designated area. This time must be spent quietly thinking about your behavior and how to resolve the problem. After you have refocused, you will need to process the situation requiring this intervention and healthy coping skills you can use as an alternative in the future.

Emergency Interventions

Seclusion - Seclusion is when you are physically prevented from leaving an area. This intervention is the result of your choice to act out in a way that is dangerous to yourself or to others and safety must be ensured.

Restraint - When you make the choice to become physically aggressive toward yourself or others, staff may have to physically restrain you until you are able to calm down and make healthier choices about your behavior.

Special Interventions - A special intervention specific for a resident may be developed if a pattern of behaviors in a certain conduct area persists. The special intervention is unique to the situation and will be in addition to other reward or consequence interventions.


Unit Restriction - Unit Restriction means that you may not leave the unit due to dangerous behaviors: you must eat on the unit, you are not able to attend outings or go on TTVs, and you cannot attend groups off the unit. This is for your safety.

Precautions

When a resident acts inappropriately in a way that requires special measures to monitor her, she will be placed on precautions. If a resident is placed on precautions during her stay, she may forfeit her Phase for that week and is unable to participate in TTVs and/or outings. These are the possible precautions:

Assault (A) - Physical aggression, posturing and serious verbal threats

Suicide (S) - Threats, gestures, and attempts to harm self

Sharps (SH) – Current or recent self-harming behavior, attempt, or gesture which would result in loss of functioning or disfigurement.

Elopement (E) - Any attempt or successful fleeing from facility or any questionable behavior or history that might suggest risk of running away from the facility

Sexual Aggression/Acting Out (SA) - Sexually explicit notes or any physical contact of a sexual nature

Homicidal (H) – Current or recent homicidal behavior, attempt, gesture, verbalized intent, or homicidal behavior directed towards another person.

Family Participation:

Your Bridge between Treatment & Home


Therapeutic Trial Visits (TTVs)

TTVs are opportunities for the patients to spend time with their family to work on treatment goals. It is important to show that you are able to apply the positive behaviors that you learned during treatment to your relationships within your family and community. TTVs are ordered only by your physician, after approval from your therapist, family, probation officer (if applicable) and a thorough discussion by the treatment team.

  • You must have had at least one family therapy session with your therapist before going on a TTV.

  • TTVs are for you to spend time with your family or guardian not alone with friends. You are to always be supervised by the person named on your TTV request form.

  • A request for a TTV with goals listed must be filled out by Tuesday of the week requested. TTV requests will be decided in treatment team meetings with your physician.

  • Your TTV form must be filled out by you and your guardian each time you return to the building, to assess your progress on established TTV goals.

The length of your TTV will be determined individually based upon a decision reached by the treatment team, your guardian, your therapist or probation officer/court (if applicable).



Medical, dental, eye appointments outside of Brynn Marr Hospital:

Patients in our care are likely to leave the facility for medical, dental, and/or eye appointments. Parents/guardians are required to escort their child to these scheduled appointments. Patients benefit most from access to the community and they need as many opportunities possible to demonstrate success outside of the facility. TTVs for medical, dental, and/or eye appointments will be granted based on the patient’s safety and the emergency of the appointment if the patient is unsafe.



Visitation/Calls

Visitation Schedule:

Monday – Thursday 4:30pm-5:30pm

Visitation Policies

  • Please call 910-577-1400 or ask a staff member for the most updated information regarding our current visitation.

  • Visitation is for 20 minutes at a time

  • Only 2 people may visit at a time

  • All visitors must be 18 years or older

  • All visitors must have a valid photo ID present and Patient ID number

  • NO cell phones, electronic devices, cigarettes/lighters, bags/purses, or food are permitted beyond the main lobby

  • Our clinical staff delivers individual and group therapy throughout the day and will not be available to meet with visitors. Clinical staff meetings are by appointment only.

  • No one under the age of 18 is to be left unattended in the hospital lobby or permitted in the visitation areas.


Telephone Schedule: Monday through Sunday (6:30pm – 8:00pm)

Special visitation and calls will be determined on an individual basis by your Therapist. All visitation and calls must be pre-approved by your guardian and are only at scheduled times; unless otherwise scheduled by the therapist. No calls will be placed or accepted to/from unauthorized people. Incoming calls from people other than your family/guardian will only be permitted if from caseworkers, probation officers, clergy, and attorneys.

Mail

Letter writing is encouraged to build social skills and support systems. Residents have the right to send/receive unopened mail that may be restricted for valid safety reasons as documented in the patient’s medical record and that the legal responsible person will be notified if it becomes necessary to restrict a patient’s rights. Restrictions will be reviewed on a weekly basis and expire within 30 days unless reviewed and renewed in writing. Recipients of all incoming and outgoing mail must be approved by the guardian and must be listed on the call/visitation list. All unauthorized incoming mail will be given to your guardian or held until the time of your discharge. Mail will be received and distributed by your therapist. Mail will be monitored by the therapist at their discretion. Letter writing to another Resident or patient at Brynn Marr Hospital while you are a patient here is prohibited.



Points of Interest



Hygiene

Hygiene is an expectation to be completed in the mornings at the start of your day and in the evenings at the end of your day. At each time, you are expected to checkout your hygiene bin with staff and checked it back in to staff before you go to your next group/programming activity. Everyone is expected to wash up and brush their teeth at least twice daily. You will be assigned a designated time and are expected to shower in the evening. If you should need additional hygiene time, it will be assessed by the unit nurse.

***Remember *** - good hand washing is an important part of hygiene – it is expected that you will wash your hands before meals, after using the restroom, and often throughout the day.

Room Checks

Room checks are done multiple times daily in each room by staff. It is important for every resident on the unit to take responsibility and pride in their space. Please follow the checklist below:

  • Bed is made with a bottom and top sheet, and a pillow in a pillow case (linens for your bed are handed out weekly).

  • Your toilet is flushed and all towels and wash cloths in the hamper.

  • Clothes are picked up, folded and placed neatly on the shelves or in your cubby. Unclean clothes are placed in the clothes basket.

  • The floor and other surfaces are free of clutter and trash.

  • Under no circumstances should you have unauthorized items in your room, such as those items found on the contraband list.

  • Your nightstand must be cleaned and organized with no overflowing mess.


If you do not have a roommate, it is your sole responsibility to maintain the cleanliness of your room. If you do have a roommate, you will only be responsible for your portion of the room and your belongings. The bathroom is a shared responsibility as well.

Laundry

The laundry schedule is posted on the unit. Please check your name / room number for your assigned laundry days. You are responsible for doing your own personal laundry on your designated laundry day. If you have no clean clothes, you will be provided with a clean hospital gown to wear. Please note: hospital gowns can NOT be worn off the unit for any reason to include school and the cafeteria for meals. You will not be on unit restriction. However, you will not be able to leave the unit until you have clean clothes to wear. If you have no clean clothes and are unable to go to the cafeteria due to your choices, you will be provided a hot tray.

*You may wash your clothes even if it is not your laundry day. However, you must first wait for the other patients to wash their clothes, as it is not your day.

Birthdays

Birthdays are a very special time in our lives. We will celebrate each patient’s special day.



TV/ Movie Time

Only approved TV channels will be allowed, these include Discovery Channel, Discovery Health, ESPN, Animal Planet, National Geographic, Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, History Channel, Food Network and all news channels.

  • TV is watched only during appropriate times as listed on the posted schedule.

  • The remote will only be handled by staff.

  • G and PG rated movies be appropriate for all ages to watch; PG-13 movies must pre-approved by Nursing Supervisors or Therapists.

Meal Times

Meal times are an opportunity for you to practice appropriate social skills and healthy eating habits.

Behavioral Expectations:

  1. Prior to entering the hallway outside the unit, you must be in a straight line and lined up quietly according to room order/bed order.

  2. There are to be no conversations during transitions on and off the unit.

  3. Once lined up, the line is expected to remain straight.

  4. Once entering the dining room, you are required to leave enough space (arm’s length) between yourself and the person in front of you. There is no eating in line.

  5. You must follow any prescribed diet or meal plan ordered by your physician or dietician.

  6. If you are wearing a green ID band, you are required to line up at the end of the line so that dietary staff are able to provide the appropriate foods for your specialized diet.

  7. Once seated in your assigned seat, changing seats is not allowed.

  8. Table conversation is permitted; however, the volume is expected to remain low and content appropriate. Conversing with residents on other units is not ever allowed.

  9. You are not allowed to share or pass food among your peers.

  10. You are responsible for your own tray. You are not to dispose of anyone else's tray or trash.

  11. You are responsible for your own utensils; they must be turned in to the MHT following every meal. You are not to turn in anyone else’s utensils.

  12. You must always ask permission before leaving your seat for any reason.

  13. You will be encouraged to make well-rounded healthy food choices.

  14. Those restricted to eating on the unit will be provided with 3 meals from the cafeteria.

  15. Double portions are only given with a physician’s order.

  16. Three snacks are provided daily.

  17. Seconds are allowed on vegetables, salad items, or a sandwich only unless otherwise ordered by the physician.

  18. If you choose to remain on the unit for a meal(s), you will be provided with cold options on the unit (i.e. cereal, sandwich, etc.).

  19. Those on bed rest or “sick bed” will be given a clear liquid diet for that day.

Court Hearing Process

Minor residents (anyone under 17 years of age or younger who is not married or legally emancipated) admitted on either a Voluntary or Involuntary basis to Brynn Marr Hospital must have a Court hearing before a District Court Judge within fifteen (15) days following admission. This hearing is required by North Carolina General Statute 122C-224.

For residents admitted to Brynn Marr Hospital by midnight on Monday, the virtual Court hearing will be scheduled for Friday of the same week. For residents admitted after midnight on Monday, the virtual Court hearing will be scheduled for Friday of the week following admission.

Persons who are named as a Petitioner in Involuntary Commitment proceedings will receive a Notice of Hearing from the Onslow County Clerk of Court which will give information regarding the scheduled Court date and time. Petitioners are encouraged to attend scheduled hearings; failure to appear at the hearings may result in the Judge ordering a subpoena compelling the appearance at a hearing scheduled following a one-week postponement.

Virtual hearings are held at Brynn Marr Hospital on Friday mornings beginning at 10:00am. The hearings are heard privately and individually before a District Court Judge. An attorney will be appointed, at no cost to the patient or family, to represent the patient at the Court hearing. The resident or the legally responsible person may request a privately retained attorney to represent the resident at the hearing; the expenses incurred for the services of the privately retained attorney will be the responsibility of the resident or legally responsible person.

If the resident is discharged from Brynn Marr Hospital prior to the scheduled Court date, the hearing is cancelled and the resident and legally responsible person are not required to participate in the virtual hearing.

Persons planning to attend virtual Court hearings are asked to be available promptly by 9:45am so that hearings may begin according to schedule. The number of hearings scheduled for Fridays will vary from week to week; therefore, persons attending hearings should be prepared for a waiting period of one (1) to three (3) hours to conclude.

If you have any questions regarding the virtual Court hearing process, or are unable to attend the scheduled hearing, please contact the Onslow County Clerk of Superior Court between 8:00am and 5:00pm Monday through Friday by calling (910) 478-3600.













Resident’s Bill of Rights


I. FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS:

Each resident shall at all times retain the right to:

  1. Be treated with dignity and respect.

  2. To receive the utmost professional care without regard to race, color, sex, national origin,

source of payment, sexual preference, age, or handicap.

  1. Full citizenship (except as excluded by law).

  2. Application for a Writ of Habeas Corpus.

  3. Petition of Judicial Release.

  4. Access to legal counsel and private physicians of his choice at his expense.

  5. Explanation of status, rules, regulations and restrictions, and treatment including medication and how they apply to his condition.

  6. Explanation of available grievance and appeal procedures.

  1. TREATMENT RIGHTS:

Each resident shall at all times retain the right to:

  1. Be free from physical, emotional, and verbal abuse.

  2. Nursing and medical assessment, within 24 hours after admission, including assessment of pain

  3. Prompt and adequate medical attention for physical illness and emergency procedures and to expect that when medically indicated transfer to another healthcare facility.

  4. Good quality care provided by competent staff with high professional standards that are continually maintained and reviewed.

  5. Proper and adequate medication and an explanation of the risks and possible side effects of all medications.

  6. The least restrictive conditions necessary to achieve adequate care and treatment and notification of alternative procedures.

  7. A treatment program planned to meet individual needs.

  8. Know the name, title, and function of all staff persons concerned with treatment provided.

  9. Provision of proper, safe, and sanitary shelter, appealing and nutritious food, and security in self and personal possessions.

  10. The opportunity for periodic consultation with clinicians not directly responsible for the treatment program.

  11. To refuse any drugs, treatment or procedure offered by the facility to the extent permitted by law. The physician shall inform the resident of her rights to refuse any drugs, treatment, or procedures and of the medical consequences of the resident’s refusal of any drugs, treatment, or procedure.

  12. The right to full information in laymen’s terms, concerning diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis, including information about alternative treatments and possible complications. When it is not possible or medically advisable to give such information to the resident, the information shall be given on his behalf to the resident’s designee.

  13. To expect reasonable continuity of care, inclusive of a written discharge plan, and to be advised by the treatment staff.

  14. The right to every consideration of personal privacy concerning the medical care program.

  15. Case discussion, consultation, examination, and treatment are considered confidential and will be conducted discretely.

  16. To medical and nursing treatment that avoids duplication of services and unnecessary physical and mental discomfort.

  17. Except for emergencies, the physician must obtain the necessary informed consent prior to the start of any procedure and/or treatment.


  1. COMMUNICATION RIGHTS:

  1. Each resident shall at all times retain the right to:

  1. Send and receive sealed mail and have access to writing material, limited postage, and staff assistance when necessary. The therapist will distribute mail to the resident. All mail received must be opened in front of staff to ensure resident’s safety as well as the safety of other residents and staff.

  2. Contact and consult with legal counsel and private physicians of his/her choice and at his/her expense.

  3. Provision of interpreters for certain individuals who speak languages other than English, and use of alternative communication techniques for those who are deaf or blind.

  1. Each minor resident may at all reasonable times:

  1. Communicate and consult with the agency or individual having legal custody of him/her.

  2. Communicate and consult with legal counsel and private mental health or mental retardation specialist of his/her legal custodian or guardian’s choice, at his/her expense.

  1. Expect to be informed of the use of tape recorders, audiovisuals, or other such equipment and to be ensured of confidentiality.

  2. Expect to receive a detailed explanation of his/her bill and to receive full information and counseling on availability of known financial resources.

  3. A resident has the right to expect that the facility will provide a mechanism whereby he/she is informed upon discharge of his/her continuing health care requirements following discharge and the means for meeting them.

  4. The resident cannot be denied the right of access to an individual or agency that is authorized to act on his/her behalf to assert or protect the rights set out in this section.


IV. CONFIDENTIALITY:

Each resident shall at all times retain the right to:

  1. Have all records pertaining to his/her medical care treated as confidential except as otherwise provided by law or third party contractual arrangements.

  2. Expect that the confidentiality of alcohol and drug abuse patient records maintained by this facility is protected by Federal law and regulations. Generally, the staff may not disclose that a resident attends the program, or disclose any information identifying a resident unless:

  1. The resident consents in writing.

  2. The disclosure is allowed by a court order.

  1. Expect that the facility shall provide a resident, or resident’s designee, upon request, access to all information contained in the resident’s medical records. The resident’s attending physician may restrict a resident’s access to medical records. If the physician restricts the resident’s access to information in the medical record, the physician shall record the reasons in the resident’s medical record. Access shall be restricted only for sound medical reason. A resident’s designee may have access to the information in the resident’s medical records even if the attending physician restricts the resident’s access to those records.

  2. Federal law and regulations do not protect all information about a crime committed by a resident either at the program or against any person who works for the program or about any threat to commit such a crime.

  3. Federal laws and regulations allow for reporting suspected child abuse or neglect to appropriate State or local authorities (See 42 U.S.C. 29Odd-3 and 42 U.S.C. 290ee-3 for Federal laws and 42 CFR Part 2 for Federal regulations).

  4. Please be advised that Disability Rights North Carolina (DRNC) may visit our facility from time to time. DRNC is the federally mandated Protection and Advocacy System (P&A) for the State of North Carolina. Congress created the P&A System to monitor compliance with respect to the rights and safety of residents, and provide information and training about individual rights and the P&A system. DRNC may visit our facility for monitoring purposes, which simply means that they will tour our facility, talk with residents and staff, and observe the general atmosphere of our facility. Brynn Marr and DRNC want to ensure that the parents and guardians of individuals in the care of the facility are informed that the P&A will be conducting these monitoring activities and, in the course of such monitoring, may speak informally to those with a legal guardian. If you have any questions concerning DRNC or its monitoring activities, you may contact them at (877) 235-4210 (toll free) or at www.disabilityrightsnc.org


V. ADDITIONAL RIGHTS:

  1. Each resident shall at all times retain the right to:

  1. Make and receive confidential telephone calls during appropriate phone call times outside of school instruction and structured group activities.

  2. Receive visitors during visiting hours. The resident and/or legally responsible party have the right to consent to receive the visitors he/she designates, including, but not limited to: a spouse, a domestic partner (including a same-sex domestic partner), another family member, or a friend, and to withdraw or deny such consent at any time.

  3. Before the resident is furnished medical care, if possible, the resident shall also have the right to designate a Support Person who can exercise the resident’s visitation rights in the event the resident is incapacitated or otherwise unable to do so. Resident visitation rights shall not be restricted, limited, or otherwise denied by the hospital on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, or disability. All visitors shall enjoy full and equal visitation privileges consistent with the resident’s preferences. The Hospital may impose clinically appropriate limitations on resident visitation when visitation would interfere with the resident’s care, whether the reason for limiting or restricting visitation is infection control, disruptive behavior of visitors, or the resident’s need for rest or privacy.

  4. Not be awakened by staff unless it is medically or clinically necessary.

  5. Make visits outside unless such resident is committed to this hospital under the Mental Health Statutes of this State.

  6. Be out of doors and have access to facilities and equipment for physical exercise several times a week.

  7. Keep and use his/her own clothing and personal possessions unless otherwise deemed a safety concern by the facility.

  8. Know what facility rules and regulations apply to his/her conduct as a resident.

  9. Be free of exploitation.

  10. Be free of unwarranted suspension or expulsion from services.

  11. Participate in religious worship.

  12. Keep and spend a reasonable amount of money.

  13. Each adult patient shall, at all times, retain the right to retain a motor vehicle driver’s license, unless otherwise prohibited by the General Statutes of this State.

  14. Each adult patient shall, at all times, retain the right to exercise all civil rights, including the right to dispose of property, execute instruments, make purchases, enter into contractual relationships, register, and vote, and marry and obtain divorce, unless such patient has been adjudicated incompetent under the provisions of the General Statutes of this state and has not been restored to legal capacity; provided; however, that this shall be construed as validating the act of any patient who was at the time of the act, in fact, incompetent.

  15. Expect to be informed of program specific rules and regulations at the time of entry into the service.


  1. ADDITIONAL RIGHTS AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF MINORS:

(17 years of age or younger)

  1. No minor resident shall be expected to exercise rights and privileges, nor shall be accorded responsibilities that by law are generally accepted practices reserved or limited to adult choices.

  1. Parents and guardians must be kept informed of the management of all aspects of the resident’s living situation by staff members in their function in loco parentis. However, no resident shall be denied or deprived of the rights applicable to all citizens as guaranteed by law.

  2. Each minor resident shall have the right to:

  1. Receive special education and vocational training in addition to other forms of treatment.

  2. Participate in recreation, physical exercise, and outdoor activity on a regular basis, in accordance with individual needs.

  3. Receive such assistance as needed in sending and receiving correspondence and making telephone calls.

  4. Receive visitors under appropriate supervision. Such visiting is not to take precedence over school or therapy.

  5. Have access to individual storage space for his/her own use.


VII.RESTRICTION OF RESIDENT PRIVILEGES:

Restriction of resident privileges may be initiated upon a physician’s order when the life and safety of the resident, staff or therapeutic environment is at risk.

  1. The goal of the restrictive action is to be therapeutic and not punitive.

  2. Restrictions of privileges are done in progressive sequence and based on the resident’s behavior, first implementing less restrictive measures.

  3. Restrictions of privileges are done in consultation with treatment team members and the attending physicians.

  4. Types of Restrictions:

  1. Loss of phone or visiting privileges.

  2. Restricted to the building.

  3. Restricted to the unit.

  4. Restricted to the room.

  5. Restricted to the quiet room.

  6. Restricted from using particular area (i.e. courtyard, gym)
